summary: Refineries are still running below last year after the Hormuz disruption, 2026 is on course for a record or near-record year as a strong El Niño builds, and adaptation money for poorer countries has stalled ahead of COP31.

news.title: Global refinery runs fell 6% in spring after the Hormuz disruption and are still 5% below last year
news.tldr: The US Energy Information Administration says world crude oil input to refineries fell 4.8 million barrels per day in the second quarter of 2026 and had recovered only partly by the third quarter.
news.why_selected: A primary-source measure of how far the Middle East conflict and attacks on Russian facilities have cut the capacity that turns crude into fuels, with a stated link to record diesel prices.

sections.heading: Context
sections.body: A refinery turns crude oil into fuels such as gasoline, diesel and jet fuel, so the crude that refineries take in, called refinery inputs, shows how much fuel the world can make. Inputs normally rise in the second and third quarters as plants finish maintenance. In 2025 they rose by 0.3 million barrels per day (b/d) in the second quarter and 2 million b/d in the third.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.body: In an analysis based on data from the commercial tracker Kpler, the EIA reports that global crude inputs fell by 4.8 million b/d, or 6%, in the second quarter of 2026, after conflict began in the Middle East in late February. They rose by 1.8 million b/d in the third quarter but stayed about 5% below the same period of 2025. China's inputs fell by 2.1 million b/d in the second quarter and by a further 0.8 million b/d in the third. India, South Korea and Japan together fell by more than 1.0 million b/d, then regained 0.8 million b/d. Inputs in Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates each fell by 0.7 million b/d, because the closure of the Strait of Hormuz limited exports of refined products. Russian inputs fell by 0.6 million b/d and then by 0.8 million b/d as attacks on its oil infrastructure continued. US inputs rose by 0.5 million b/d in each of the two quarters.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: Fuel prices depend on refining capacity as well as on crude supply. The EIA says the loss of Russian output, on top of reduced refining in Asia and the Middle East, hit global diesel markets that were already tight and contributed to diesel reaching its highest nominal price on record in September. The agency also notes that the United States increasingly exported refined products to make up for lost supply.

sections.heading: What to watch
sections.body: Whether third-quarter recovery continues as more crude moves through the Strait of Hormuz and alternative routes, whether attacks on Russian facilities persist, and the EIA's next monthly outlook.

news.title: 2026 is on course to tie or beat 2024 as the warmest year, with a record El Niño building, Carbon Brief finds
news.tldr: Carbon Brief's quarterly analysis of six temperature datasets says 2026 will be the warmest or second-warmest year, and projects that a record El Niño will make 2027 the warmest year with 96% probability.
news.why_selected: A clear, number-rich update on the global temperature record from a specialist outlet, with an explicit split between observed data and its own projections.

sections.heading: Context
sections.body: Global temperature is tracked by several groups that use different methods, so they can rank a year differently. El Niño is the warm phase of a recurring climate pattern in the tropical Pacific that releases ocean heat into the atmosphere and temporarily raises global temperatures. Human-caused greenhouse gas emissions drive the long-term warming; El Niño and La Niña add year-to-year swings. The previous annual record was set in 2024.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.body: Carbon Brief, a climate-science news site, analysed records from six groups. August 2026 was the warmest August in all six, by about 0.12C on average, and September was the second warmest September, behind 2023. January to September ran about 1.45C above pre-industrial levels, second only to 2024 and around 0.06C below it. El Niño broke the daily Nino3.4 region record in September, set in 2015, and has stayed above it since. As of 18 October the daily value was about 3.5C above the 1996-2025 average, about 0.4C above the 2015 peak. Roughly 22% of the world's surface had its warmest July-September, and Western Europe had its hottest summer on record. Projections are Carbon Brief's own: 2026 ends near 1.52C with a 67% chance of beating 2024, while forecasts peak El Niño at around 4C in December. It projects 2027 at about 1.7C, with a 96% chance of a record.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: The datasets disagree: a 2026 record is likely in Berkeley Earth and NASA GISTEMP, too close to call in three others and unlikely in the European ERA5, so January headlines may differ. Global temperatures lag the Pacific by about three months, so the biggest effect lands in 2027. Carbon Brief also reports that Earth's energy imbalance has more than doubled since the 2000s, to around 1.25 watts per square metre over the past decade. Heat of this kind raises electricity demand, strains grids and stresses crops.

sections.heading: What to watch
sections.body: Official January annual rankings from each dataset, the December El Niño peak and 2027 monthly records.

news.title: Adaptation finance for developing countries has stalled, UN report says, ahead of COP31
news.tldr: UNEP's 2026 Adaptation Gap Report finds international adaptation finance at most $32 billion in 2024, flat or falling since 2022, against a need of $305 billion a year by 2035, according to the Guardian.
news.why_selected: A UN assessment that sets the money debate for COP31, with concrete numbers on the gap between promises and need.

sections.heading: Context
sections.body: Adaptation means preparing for climate impacts already under way, for example by building flood defences, early warning systems and drought-resilient irrigation. Wealthy nations promised support for poorer ones in 2021, and the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) publishes an annual Adaptation Gap Report on progress. Its 2026 edition is titled Ready? Not, and UNEP says it finds that adaptation finance keeps falling short of needs.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.body: The Guardian's account of the report gives these figures. UNEP estimates the 155 developing nations will need $305 billion a year by 2035. International public flows were at most $32 billion in 2024, only about $1 billion above 2023 and below the 2022 peak, partly because European governments are shifting budgets to defence. That is behind the goal of $40 billion by 2025, although multilateral development banks may have closed part of the gap last year. At COP30 in Belem, Brazil, wealthy nations agreed to triple adaptation finance by 2035 to between $85 billion and $120 billion, which would meet only 20-29% of needs. Least developed countries need $40-50 billion a year, about 3-4% of their GDP, yet received 16% less in 2024 than two years earlier. A new loss and damage fund received requests totalling $2.8 billion from 119 countries against initial funding of $342 million. UNEP's executive director Inger Andersen said an overshoot above 1.5C is now locked in.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: Money is the main unresolved issue for many poorer countries. Low- and middle-income countries accounted for 99% of the 765 million people affected by floods and landslides between 2020 and 2025. The report also notes that debt and equity costs can more than double adaptation project budgets, which is why climate justice groups want grants or concessional loans rather than high-interest loans for sea walls and heat shelters that earn no revenue.

sections.heading: What to watch
sections.body: COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, from 9 to 20 November, and whether donors set new adaptation finance commitments.

papers.title: Zero emissions commitment depends on warming level
papers.tldr: In UK Earth System Model simulations, temperature stays roughly flat after emissions stop if warming is 2 degrees or less, but keeps rising by 0.4-0.6 degrees over 150 years from 3 to 5 degrees.
papers.why_selected: It tests the common assumption that warming stops when emissions reach zero, with direct bearing on carbon budgets and overshoot.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.body: When human carbon dioxide emissions stop, global temperature does not level off at once. The temperature change that follows is called the zero emissions commitment (ZEC). It matters for how much carbon the world can still emit for a given temperature limit, and for whether warming can be reversed. Until now it was not known how the ZEC depends on how warm the planet already is when emissions stop.

sections.heading: Existing approaches
sections.body: The IPCC Special Report on 1.5C assumed the ZEC was about zero over decades, based on sparse evidence from a few models. A later model comparison, ZECMIP, used 18 Earth system models and found the ZEC near zero after moderate cumulative emissions but with larger spread after higher emissions. Its standard experiment did not sample the higher warming levels examined here.

sections.heading: Key idea
sections.body: The authors used one model, the UK Earth System Model version 1.2. They raised emissions at a constant 8 petagrams of carbon per year, producing about 2 degrees of warming per century, then cut emissions to zero at warming levels from 1.5 to 5 K, and tracked temperature. A simple two-layer energy-balance model separated two competing effects: continued warming because the climate is still out of balance, and cooling as land and ocean absorb CO2. At higher warming, the land carbon uptake saturates, and because CO2's warming effect depends on the fractional change in concentration, a given drawdown cuts radiative forcing less when background CO2 is high.

sections.heading: Results
sections.body: At 1.5-2 K the ZEC stays close to zero, consistent with ZECMIP and the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report. At higher levels temperature keeps rising by about 0.15-0.2 K per century, reaching roughly 0.4-0.6 K after 150 years at 3-5 K. CO2 falls by 76 ppm after 150 years at 5 K versus 45 ppm at 1.5 K, yet that is not enough to offset the extra warming.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: The finding suggests stabilising or reversing warming gets harder as peak temperature rises, which weakens the case for relying on temporary overshoot. The main caveat is that these results come from a single Earth system model, three ensemble members per case, and idealised emission cuts.
